title_original: In a Sydney gallery, Philippe Parreno’s art is powered by a desert 17,000km away
excerpt_original: In the Museum of Contemporary Art, the French artist’s first major Australian show is truly unpredictable – influenced by real-time data coming from a Spanish farm I’m standing in a massive white-cube space, staring at a perplexing assortment of objects. There are several…

blocks.text: I ’m standing in a massive white-cube space, staring at a perplexing assortment of objects. There are several expensive looking lamps; a massive industrial fan; a couple of speakers; marquee-style lights; a glowing assemblage of power adapters. At the back of the gallery, a silvery light slides up and down a pole. The bulbs are flickering erratically, and there’s a low hum of machine noise, overlaid with bird song and distant barking.
As an installation, taken by itself, it’s deceptively underwhelming – a spectacle without a story.

blocks.alt: Gallery installation with glowing chandeliers, crystal pendant lights and dark glass sphere clusters
blocks.caption: ‘Deceptively underwhelming’ … entering Philippe Parreno’s exhibition 5 Moons at the Museum of Contemporary Art, Sydney. Photograph: Rémi Chauvin/The Guardian

blocks.text: This will be visitors’ first encounter with the Museum of Contemporary Art’s summer blockbuster exhibition, Philippe Parreno: 5 Moons, named for the five lunar cycles of the show’s duration. It’s the first major Australian exhibition by the acclaimed French contemporary artist, renowned for taking over museums and galleries – including Tate Modern’s Turbine Hall and the Palais de Tokyo in Paris – with discombobulating and delightful kinetic arrangements of objects, screen works, sound and lighting.
Parreno’s medium of choice is the exhibition itself; he creates holistic, unpredictable environments for the visitor to navigate.

blocks.alt: At Philippe Parreno’s “5 Moons” exhibition, a person walks past a piano among hanging inflatable fish balloons
blocks.caption: Installation photographs of Philippe Parreno’s new exhibition 5 Moons at the Museum of Contemporary Art in Sydney. Photograph: Rémi Chauvin/The Guardian

blocks.text: At the MCA, Parreno has created a series of connected environments across the museum’s three levels, featuring works made over his four-decade career.

Upstairs, there’s an orange-carpeted gallery populated by floating, helium-filled, fish-shaped balloons in citrus tones, in which a grand piano plays an enigmatic score. On another floor, a giant luminescent cuttlefish gazes out impassively from a screen, its fins and arms gently undulating, as ambient electronic noise emanates from large swiveling speaker banks.
These spaces feel like haunted houses; machines operated by ghosts or powered by supernatural energy.

blocks.alt: A ghostly cloud-like sculpture glows white in Philippe Parreno’s dark, red-lit installation space
blocks.caption: Inside Parreno’s MCA show 5 Moons. Photograph: Rémi Chauvin/The Guardian

blocks.text: In fact, they’re powered by nature: real-time data – including wind speed, humidity and temperature – captured on sensors on an abandoned almond farm in the Tabernas desert in south-eastern Spain, a region best known internationally as the backdrop to spaghetti westerns such as The Good, the Bad and the Ugly and Once Upon a Time in the West.
Data from the farm has been reconfigured into an algorithm that influences the sound, air flow and lighting 17,000km away in Sydney . The land is improvising a score, and the museum is playing it.

blocks.alt: An 11-hour film of footage of Parreno’s abandoned almond farm.
blocks.caption: An 11-hour film of footage of Parreno’s almond farm in Spain. Photograph: Rémi Chauvin/The Guardian

blocks.text: In a darkened gallery on the museum’s third floor, a massive screen is showing an 11-hour film composed of footage shot on the abandoned almond farm. Visitors can, if they choose, sit and watch a night pass under the Spanish moon.

Live sound from this terrain is also played in the gallery, making for an uncanny mix: during my visit, nocturnal insect noises from Spain are punctuated by the toot of an ocean liner docked outside in Sydney Harbour.

“What I normally try to do for exhibition is to try to create sort of a milieu, or an ecosystem, where things are responding to each other,” says Parreno, whose family migrated from the same region of Spain hundreds of years ago, to Algeria, where he was born.

blocks.alt: A bald man stands in a corridor amid floating red fish balloons
blocks.caption: ‘In the system we live in, you are always obliged to respond to a signal. Here you are not’ … Parreno, in the MCA. Photograph: Rémi Chauvin/The Guardian

blocks.text: Backstory is important for Parreno’s art: without it, his ecosystems risk seeming frustratingly opaque or worse, inane.

Some parts of the MCA exhibition stand alone, without narrative, thanks to their aesthetic or mise en scene. Some are more tenuous: a white-walled area in which a layer of helium filled speech-bubble balloons covers the ceiling, while a series of coloured lights flash. When you learn the lighting pattern is a morse code translation of a mystical adventure by French writer René Daumal, it suddenly feels more substantial.

Parreno’s most famous artwork, his 2016 takeover of the Tate’s Turbine Hall, delighted some and frustrated others. But his backstory, involving a jar of yeast in a hidden lab whose biodata was influencing the whole thing, was almost irresistibly intriguing.
“Lots of the things I do require people to endorse a fiction,” Parreno commented at the time .

His interest in fiction is more than a gimmick, it’s deeply philosophical, and 5 Moons is underpinned by ideas of how our perceptions of a thing change it; how the way we imagine land, by knock on effect, influences and transforms it.

When Parreno showed an earlier iteration of the 5 Moons film at Munich’s Haus der Kunst in 2024, he said the work was designed to feel as if the land was “speaking to you”. “With the ways climate change is changing the world, how do we address the landscape? Are we going to keep transforming it? Or is it maybe the other way around – that the land is looking at us.”
When he started out making exhibitions in the late 80s and 90s, Parreno had revolutionary ideals. “You want to change the world. You want to produce a new reality,” he tells me.

And now? “I want to create that thing that you don’t see much [these days],” he says. “In the system we live in, you are always obliged to respond to a signal. Here you are not. You just float with your own attention, and you spend the time you want.”
Philippe Parreno: 5 Moons is on at the Museum of Contemporary Art, Sydney, until 26 April 2027
